world.bio: Taught geography at a comprehensive in north London for thirty-four years. Retired three years ago and now spend my time between an allotment, a choir and, at the moment, my late father's Highgate flat, which I am clearing out. He was a Foreign Office China hand in the 1960s, and I keep finding things I can't name.
skills_assets: Thirty-four years of teaching geography; very good with maps, archives and patient with detail
An allotment plot in Archway and a Saturday habit of weeding it
Alto in a local community choir
Access to my father's papers, photographs and the contents of his flat
A daughter who is a solicitor and handles the legal side of the estate

projects.name: Clearing the Highgate flat
projects.text: The flat has to be empty by the end of November. So far I've done the kitchen, the hall cupboard and most of the books. The study is still untouched: letters from Hong Kong, a box of slides, rolled scrolls I can't read, and a long wooden instrument in a faded cloth bag. I posted a photo of the instrument online, described as 'a long wooden zither with no frets, seven strings and cracked lacquer', asking what it is. And, in a second post, who repairs fretless instruments.

projects.name: Allotment winter prep
projects.text: Digging in manure, covering the beds, and a long-running war with slugs. This year I'm trying a ring of crushed eggshells and an upturned beer trap, with mixed results.

notes.text: Spent the whole afternoon in the study. Found letters from Hong Kong from 1964 addressed to 'Dear Teddy', and a photograph of Dad in a Mao-collar jacket standing beside a pagoda. I never knew him in that jacket. It's like clearing someone else's flat.

The long instrument in the bag. About a metre and twenty, dark wood, seven silk strings, no frets, lacquer cracked like a dry riverbed. I don't know what it is. I put a photo online. Someone replied 'looks Chinese, maybe antique' and someone else 'are you selling?' No and no, I think.

Daughter Anna came over. She wants me to consign the lot to auction: she says it's tidier. Two auction houses came to look at the instrument and offered consignment. I told Anna I'd rather it be played again than sold. She sighed and said, 'Mum, you can't even say what it is.' Fair.

Choir rehearsal for the winter concert. We're doing the Holst, 'In the Bleak Midwinter'. I always cry at the second verse. The conductor said my alto line was lovely; I told him it's because I'm old and wet.

A dealer came round, looked at the instrument for two minutes and said the finish looks like 'very old Chinese lacquer over cloth'. Lovely man. He told me not to varnish it or let anyone glue it. I said I wouldn't dream of it. I certainly don't want it shipped anywhere; it has been in this flat since 1971 and I don't want it going in a crate.
Grandson Oscar's gap-year plans. He wants to cycle across Central Asia. I said take proper maps. He rolled his eyes and said, 'Gran, we have phones.' The geography teacher in me died a little.
The allotment: slugs have eaten the entire row of lettuce. Eggshells did nothing. Beer trap caught 41 slugs, which I counted.

Dad's study again. Found a notebook with columns of Chinese characters in his small neat hand, and next to one of them a pencil sketch of the instrument in its bag. I can't read a word of it. I photographed the page and put it in a folder called 'Dad, unreadable'. Strange to have him turn up in a script I can't follow.
Rang the cousin in Norfolk about the funeral photographs. No one has anything. Poured a whisky and put on Dad's old LP of Chinese music that I found in the sideboard. Played it very quietly.

messages.text:
Anna: Mum, the auction house can come on Thursday.
Me: I'd like to wait.
Anna: For what?
Me: Someone to tell me what it is.

Pam: Dress rehearsal Saturday. Black and red.
Me: I've lost the red scarf.
Pam: I'll bring a spare.

Okafor: I wouldn't touch the lacquer. Nor would I let the auction house move it.
Me: Will do.
Okafor: Keep it at stable temperature, it's quite fragile.

Oscar: Gran, can I borrow your atlas?
Me: Which one?
Oscar: The big one from the 70s.
Me: Collect it Sunday, and you'll wash up.

calendar.event: Highgate flat vacated by end of month

relations.about: Daughter, solicitor, practical about the estate; wants it all tidied.
Grandson on a gap year, wants to cycle across Central Asia.

constraints: Flat must be empty by end of November
Doesn't want it shipped abroad; it is old and fragile
Limited budget for repairs, a few thousand pounds at most
sensitive: Grief about her father; she hardly knew his China years
Tension with her daughter about selling things
Feeling that much of his life is unreadable
